content:
Christians do not circumcise as a religious duty, and the reason usually given is Paul. Yet Genesis calls circumcision "an everlasting covenant", Jesus was circumcised on the eighth day, and Muslims keep the practice to this day as part of the religion of Abraham.

Paul's own record on circumcision is not one position. He forbids it to Gentile believers, calls it nothing, explains Abraham's as a seal, and in Acts circumcises a companion himself.

This article aims to provide context to that record, insha'Allah, in five passages, each set beside the Christian explanation and the Islamic practice. The Quran's command frames them: "follow the religion of Abraham, the sane in faith; he was not of the Pagans" (3:95).[1]

God says to Abraham: "Every male among you shall be circumcised ... It will be a token of the covenant between me and you", and "My covenant will be in your flesh for an everlasting covenant" (Genesis 17:10 to 13).[2] Luke records that the rite was kept for Jesus: "When eight days were fulfilled for the circumcision of the child, his name was called Jesus" (Luke 2:21).[2]

Christians answer that a new covenant has changed the duty. The question is who had the authority to change a command the Torah calls "everlasting". Islam keeps the practice. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Five practices are characteristics of the Fitra: circumcision, shaving the pubic hair, cutting the moustaches short, clipping the nails, and depilating the hair of the armpits", and: "Abraham circumcised himself after he had passed the age of eighty years."[3]

"Behold, I, Paul, tell you that if you receive circumcision, Christ will profit you nothing. Yes, I testify again to every man who receives circumcision, that he is a debtor to do the whole law" (Galatians 5:2 to 3).[2] He writes to Gentile converts who were being told to be circumcised to belong to God's people.

Scholars read the verse two ways. Paula Fredriksen argues that Paul's mission was not "Law-free": his "principled resistance to circumcising Gentiles precisely preserves these distinctions 'according to the flesh'" between Jews and Gentiles.[4] Others read in it a break with the Law itself. Both readings agree that the verse sets the covenant rite of Abraham against the benefit of Christ.

Paul tells the Galatians: "But not even Titus, who was with me, being a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised" (Galatians 2:3).[2] Acts tells of Timothy, "the son of a Jewess who believed; but his father was a Greek": Paul "took and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those parts" (Acts 16:1 to 3).[2]

The Christian explanation is that Titus was a Gentile and Timothy, through his mother, a Jew, and that Timothy's circumcision eased the mission among Jews. The account of Titus is Paul's own; the account of Timothy is Acts. On Acts' account, the man who said circumcision would make Christ "profit you nothing" performed one for the sake of the people watching.

Paul argues that Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised: "He received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had while he was in uncircumcision, that he might be the father of all those who believe, though they might be in uncircumcision" (Romans 4:11).[2]

Faith comes first in Islam too, and the Quran denies that ritual alone is righteousness (2:177).[1] It does not follow that the command given after faith lapsed. In the Quran, Abraham's faith is shown by his obedience to every command he was given: "Abraham was tried by his Lord with certain commands, which he fulfilled" (2:124).[1] We set out Paul's use of Abraham against James's in Paul and James on faith and works.

"Was anyone called having been circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised. Has anyone been called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God" (1 Corinthians 7:18 to 19).[2]

The sentence sets circumcision apart from "the commandments of God", though Genesis gives it as one of them. Peter-Ben Smit traces Paul's changing attitude across his letters, "from an attitude of strong propagation, by way of indifference and a subsequent attitude of rejection, to one of modified reintegration".[5] A teaching that moved through four positions over one man's life is hard to call a revelation that settled the matter.

The bottom line

Genesis gives circumcision as an everlasting covenant, and Jesus was circumcised on the eighth day. Paul forbade it to Gentile believers, called it nothing, made Abraham's a seal of earlier faith, and, according to Acts, circumcised Timothy himself. Smit finds his position changing across his letters; Fredriksen finds it guarding the line between Jew and Gentile.

Islam keeps the practice as part of the fitrah of Abraham and does not make it a condition of faith: a convert becomes a Muslim by belief and testimony. The disagreement is about authority, whether a command God gave Abraham could be set aside by a later teacher. The Quran answers by sending Muslims back to Abraham: "Follow the ways of Abraham the True in Faith" (16:123).[1] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Quran 2:124; 2:177; 3:95; 16:123, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  2. Genesis 17:10 to 13; Luke 2:21; Galatians 2:3; 5:2 to 3; Acts 16:1 to 3; Romans 4:11; 1 Corinthians 7:18 to 19 (World English Bible).
  3. Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Dress, the report of Abu Hurayra on the five practices of the fitrah; and Book of Asking Permission, the report of Abu Hurayra on Abraham's circumcision.
  4. Paula Fredriksen, "Judaizing the Nations: The Ritual Demands of Paul's Gospel", New Testament Studies 56, no. 2 (2010), pp. 232–252, doi:10.1017/S0028688509990294.
  5. Peter-Ben Smit, "In Search of Real Circumcision: Ritual Failure and Circumcision in Paul", Journal for the Study of the New Testament 40, no. 1 (2017), pp. 73–100, doi:10.1177/0142064X17723488.
